The understanding and precise measurement of B^0_s meson lifetimes are crucial for revealing deviations in the CKM matrix and potential signs of new physics. This study calculates the potential uncertainties in the determination of MD and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ resulting from estimated experimental errors in various lifetime measurements, specifically focusing on the LHCb experiment's current capabilities and planned upgrades, as well as the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the High-Luminosity LHC. For LHCb, precise measurements of $\Gamma_{s}$ and MD are feasible with the current setup, yielding uncertainties of 1.3% or better; in contrast, the current $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ precision is 4.0%, which can be improved to 1.4% with the upgraded detector. For the ATLAS and CMS experiments, with 300 fb^-1 of data at the High-Luminosity LHC, the achievable precision on $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ is 2.0% or better, while the $\Gamma_{s}$ precision can be 2.5% or better; combining results from all experiments at the same level of luminosity should yield a $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ precision of 1.7% or better and a $\Gamma_{s}$ precision of 2.0% or better.

This study formulates a stochastic control issue involving a linear parabolic equation affected by a control parameter affecting the coefficient, which it designates as PDE control of a fully observable Allen-Cahn equation. A unique weak solution is established for this problem when the initial and target states are given and the control domain is bounded. Furthermore, under the assumption of smooth solutions, the convergence of the discretized problem is investigated. A key aspect of this research involves developing a suitable notion of convergence for the weak scheme, which is then utilized to demonstrate the existence of a limiting solution as the discretization parameters approach zero.

Our in-depth examination of the anisotropy of the most energetic cosmic rays identifies patterns of oscillation across the entire sky. As expected, the anisotropy of these particles increases with the intensity of magnetic fields in the universe, specifically in regions with large voids. To explore the spatial distribution of cosmic rays above 4 EeV, we divided the sky into the Northern Hemisphere into nine segments. We discovered that the amplitude of the anisotropy of these particles fluctuates significantly across the sky, with variations that could be attributed to magnetic fields in the universe. Notably, the most pronounced anisotropy of cosmic rays exists along the celestial equator in the Northern Hemisphere, with an amplitude that may indicate the presence of massive voids in the universe. Compared to previous findings, the amplitude of the dipole anisotropy of cosmic rays increases with energy levels above 40 EeV, a phenomenon that has been observed in some simulations. We also detected quadrupole components of anisotropy in the Northern Hemisphere and attributed them to local magnetic fields in the Milky Way. The study of cosmic rays above 4 EeV has been expanded to include data from the Telescope Array using eight years of observations, with results showing that the amplitude of the dipole anisotropy remains consistent with previous findings.
We establish the nilpotency of a class of finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras known as Cartan-Zinbiel algebras with trivial radical, building on a previous result for solvability.

Identifying the significance of flow fluctuations within the quark-gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions remains a crucial task. Recent research involves re-examining event shape fluctuations in relation to charged particle distributions. Our current approach involves introducing a new fluctuation phenomenon related to the spatial extent of particles, known as triangular flow. Calculating triangular flow becomes increasingly complex due to the influence of non-random distribution patterns, known as flow fluctuations. Our research involves employing a newly developed four-particle cumulant correlation method to extract triangular flow fluctuations from existing LHC data. Our findings show that the magnitude of triangular flow fluctuations is directly proportional to the density of charged particles within the plasma, specifically by a factor of approximately three. Our research also demonstrates that the pattern of triangular flow fluctuations can be used to identify the shape of the quark-gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions.

This research focuses on resolving consistent query answering in databases that contain inconsistent information. To address this problem, we draw upon a logical structure that employs four truth values, originally developed by Lukasiewicz. Within this framework, we identify a subset of functions that can be used to process consistent query answering. Furthermore, we establish that the introduction of four truth values within the Lukasiewicz logic leads to an enhancement in the capabilities of the underlying logic. Specifically, this introduction enables the logic to accommodate the aforementioned subset of functions. As a result, we demonstrate that the capabilities of the logic can be equivalently replicated through the use of a more complex structure, thereby providing an alternative proof of a previous theorem.

This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a stochastic process that captures nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks in time series data featuring excess counts or zeros. TV-PARX, combining elements of the TV-PIT model and PARX model, allows for the investigation of nonlinear relationships, incorporates exogenous variables, and employs the expectation-maximization algorithm for parameter estimation. We examine the performance of TV-PARX through simulations and compare it to the TV-PIT and PARX models.

We introduce a novel neural descriptor framework known as Neural Descriptor Fields, which integrates features and descriptors through gated convolutional layers to create a unified representation for object representation and description. We further develop two primary components that leverage Neural Descriptor Fields for automated object manipulation based on instruction guidance. First, we establish a descriptor-guided automatic object manipulation framework that employs Neural Descriptor Fields in a generator and critic duo. This framework successfully masters various tasks, including the manipulation of cubes and Möbius strips, which were initially unknown to it. Second, we create a Neural Descriptor Fields-based descriptor generator that, when provided with minimal instructional examples, is able to accurately describe objects and thereby master new manipulation tasks. This descriptor generator is capable of generating descriptors that are interpretable by humans. We evaluate both models using a custom-made simulator that can manipulate two-dimensional objects in a 2D space and provide instructional guidance based on descriptor outputs. Our approach outperforms multiple baselines in terms of accuracy in a classification-based evaluation of object descriptors. The code and simulations are available at: \url{https://yilundu.github.io/projects/neural-descriptor-fields}.

Wilke constructed the d dressed numerator for QCD in three dimensions, applying the standard renormalization group approach. A non-trivial fixed point was identified, allowing the calculation of critical exponents. Comparing the results for N=4 and N=2 dimensions revealed a significant change in the value of |z_c|.

Recently, the TAP free energy has been reaffirmed as a pivotal concept in understanding the approximate message passing algorithm's behavior for integer-valued signals. By extending the TAP free energy to account for variable node noise, we derive an analogous expression relevant to binary signals. This signal-specific TAP free energy serves as a key factor in the algorithm's convergence at the threshold, as demonstrated by its direct integration into the Fyodorov-Panchenko partition function equation. Furthermore, we establish that the TAP free energy's complex phase field acts as the dual variable to the variable node noise field within the Fyodorov-Panchenko equation framework. This connection enables the introduction of a noise-to-signal transfer matrix, which facilitates the interpretation of the TAP free energy's complex phase field as a diffusion process, fueled by the noise at the variable nodes. This process's analysis yields a soft-thresholding operation as the TAP free energy's complex phase field's marginalizer. This finding is further explored to reveal the algorithm's breakdown at the information-theoretic limit, marked by a diffusion-driven phase transition of the TAP state's distribution. This knowledge can be used to devise efficient stopping criteria for the approximate message passing algorithm.

We carry out a detailed investigation into the previously unreported nighttime bright spot in the field of the SuperWASP telescope at Roque de los Muchachos Observatory, La Palma. This bright spot is attributed to light reflected off the inner surface of a telescope lens, specifically from a position near the edge of the lens. To calculate the amount of light reflected in this location, we employed a technique called image deconvolution. Furthermore, we determine the amount of light lost towards the sky in the unobstructed part of the telescope field and estimate the aerosol optical depth above the site, employing both nighttime photometry and a model. This analysis is carried out with consideration of the varying altitude of the moon and its impact on the amount of light reflected towards the sky.

Projecting 3D objects into 2D images is a fundamental task in computer vision, and object pose estimation is a key aspect of this process. A major challenge in estimating object pose arises in complex and real-world scenes where multiple objects overlap each other. To tackle this problem, researchers typically divide projections of the same object into distinct groups, effectively treating each group as a separate projection problem. In their work, the researchers investigate how projection grouping influences the estimation of object pose. They develop a framework that automatically divides projections into groups based on the projected shapes' covariance matrices. Furthermore, they explore several strategies for combining the results of the projection groups, including a weighted average and a vote-based approach. Experimental studies conducted by the researchers evaluate their approach on real-world images and synthetic data, demonstrating its effectiveness in estimating object pose. The results show that their method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in estimating object pose in challenging scenes. Key factors contributing to the performance of the method include the grouping strategy and the combination strategy used. The researchers also find that the method's performance is highly sensitive to these factors.

We introduce GLRAM, a novel extension to the Graphical Lasso framework that enables the estimation of sparse and directed graphical models from high-dimensional covariance matrices, particularly those affected by measurement errors. GLRAM formulates the Graphical Lasso problem as an optimization issue involving the sparse inverse of a matrix mean parameter, which we resolve using an iterative alternating minimization algorithm. We have established the consistency of GLRAM with regard to model specification and estimator accuracy. To accommodate the effects of measurement errors, we develop an approach based on the application of the Kronecker product and a nonlinear transformation to the t-transformation, which yields an EM-like estimator for the Gaussian distribution parameter. We have conducted both theoretical assessments of the estimator's convergence rates and related bias and variance, as well as a simulation study that compares the performance of GLRAM against other competing methods.

This study compares the computational effectiveness and precision of four numerical approaches - Langevin, Hamiltonian, Lagrangian, and reversible integration methods - in the stochastic simulation of alanine dipeptide for different time steps. The assessment of each method is evaluated through the precision of potential energy and various structural parameters of the peptide. Furthermore, the study investigates the impact of the force constant in the Hamiltonian method and the precision of the noise in the Lagrangian method. The results provide a computational benchmark for each method, enabling the selection of the most suitable approach for future peptide dihedral angle simulations.

Layered networks consist of separate layers that connect different nodes, with restrictions on how information can flow between layers. Studying these networks is crucial, as they resemble the structure of various real systems, including transportation, financial, and neurological networks. A fundamental task in network analysis is ranking nodes based on their significance, but this task becomes more complex and intriguing when networks are layered. Our research identifies how constraints between layers influence the importance of nodes and presents a mathematical approach to determine node importance in multilayer networks. This approach uses linear algebra to model the flow of information and node rankings in network networks, breaking them down into manageable components. By applying our approach to various types of networks, including a realistic model of the Brazilian electricity power grid, we show that it accurately reflects real-world systems and prioritizes nodes accordingly.
We derive the Dirac equation in the $R$-Minkowski spacetime by starting from the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime and applying a specific limit.

This study investigates the surface seal behavior of a turbine cavity subjected to water impact using high-speed imaging and pressure sensors. A specific focus is given to examining the pressure characteristics inside the cavity and how they influence the surface seal dynamics. Film-wise and jet-wise water impacts were studied and compared to surface seals influenced by these impacts. Research indicates that the pressure reduction inside the cavity increases significantly with impact speed, causing the surface seal to behave differently. At lower impact speeds, the surface seal is primarily affected by the pressure drop, but at higher speeds, the seal is affected by the sudden formation of a jet or cavitation, ultimately leading to a failure of the surface seal. Furthermore, unique bubble dynamics are observed in the case of a jet-wise water impact.

We integrate the generalized Witten effect into the spectrum of charged states in quantum gravity, exploring its implications for the relationship between the electric field and the gravitational field. We discovered that the BPS equation can be reinterpreted as a result of the interplay between the Fadde'ev-Shatashvili and Witten effects rather than a fundamental principle. Furthermore, we observed that the charged state spectrum lacks non-trivial solutions in the Minkowski background, and we identified the necessary condition for the emergence of charged states: the spacetime must possess a Killing vector field with a nonzero norm. We also examined the interplay between the Fadde'ev-Shatashvili and Witten effects in the context of the AdS7 × S3 background, uncovering the possibility of state differentiation and the related issue of state monodromy.

This research delves into the theoretical analysis of cubanite's electronic structure to provide insights into its observed charge stability and ferromagnetic ordering properties. To effectively study cubanite's complex crystal structure, we employed the Burkert-Dixon atomic displacement parameters to refine its electronic structure and subsequently investigated the effects of charge distribution models on the calculated properties. Our study highlights the significance of considering the specific crystal structure of cubanite when analyzing its electronic and molecular properties. Furthermore, we investigated the possible causes of cubanite's charge stability and ferromagnetic ordering behavior. Our results suggest that the strong covalent bonding between oxygen and metal atoms is the primary factor contributing to cubanite's charge stability, while the spin-polarized electrons and unique crystal structure together give rise to its ferromagnetic ordering behavior.

Researchers explored the interplay between light-driven quantum dynamics and acoustic vibrations within a specific type of crystal, GaAs, by shining a laser onto a quantum dot while measuring both the emitted light and acoustic resonator noise. By adjusting the laser frequency during experimentation, the team observed a predictable impact on the formation of light- matter bundles, known as photons, as well as the likelihood of these bundles being created. Furthermore, they found that the laser-driven quantum interactions could be controlled to produce unusual patterns of energy exchange between the quantum dot and the acoustic cavity. By comparing these patterns to theoretical predictions based on mathematical models, the scientists gained a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between light, matter, and sound.

Researchers have long studied lattice structures with non-orthogonal unit cell dimensions, citing Einstein's theory as a prime example. In this paper, we examine a herringbone lattice with perturbed Hamiltonian properties, subjecting it to various modifications, including commensurate phonon stopping, lattice anisotropy, dimerization, and charge disproportionation. Our findings show that all these perturbations preserve the lattice's unique feature of having only one acoustic phonon branch. On the other hand, a related lattice structure, known as the chain-ribbon lattice, was previously discovered by us and exhibits distinct acoustic optic phonon branch separation, in contrast to the herringbone lattice's counterpart.

We examine single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) generated via beam splitters and parametric amplifiers, analyzing their characteristics and practical implementation in quantum protocols. Notably, our investigation reveals that success probabilities for creating SPCCSs via beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit distinct trends, indicating that the same input conditions may yield SPCCSs with varying success rates from these two types of devices. Furthermore, we derive precise expressions for the quadrature distributions of SPCCSs generated via parametric amplifiers, which have been previously unknown. Our research also highlights that, unlike beam splitters, parametric amplifiers can produce SPCCSs with increased average coherent amplitude over the initial state, offering a potential advantage for their utilization in certain applications.

A novel numerical approach has been developed to reconstruct a polymer's configuration from statistical data, utilizing a random walk model. In this method, the polymer is represented as a trail of linked monomers, with each monomer positioned according to the probabilities derived from the data. This representation allows for the calculation of the probability distribution of any monomer's position relative to the chain's ends. This approach has been applied to a specific model featuring a Gaussian distribution of monomer positions along the chain, demonstrating accurate recovery of the original configuration.

This study presents the design of a novel unet variant, known as Dilated Dense Attention Unet, and applies it to the challenging task of esophageal tumor segmentation based on MRI scans. A comprehensive experiment is conducted to evaluate the performance of DDAUnet, alongside six competing models, on a large dataset of 138 test subjects with manually delineated tumor areas. The results demonstrate that DDAUnet outperforms the competitors in terms of overall performance, achieving Dice coefficients of 0.87, 0.83, and 0.88 in tumors, 0.84, 0.79, and 0.83 in tumors plus upper airway, and 0.78, 0.73, and 0.76 in whole body regions, respectively. Additionally, DDAUnet yields superior performance in 72% of the comparisons made.

Our proposed project aims to bridge the gap between NLP advancements and multilingual communities by developing two critical resources: a dataset of stylistically varied sentences in six languages and a unique metric for style transfer quality. To begin, we'll gather a team of native speakers from different countries to create a dataset of 20,000 sentences each in English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Portuguese. To ensure consistency across languages, we'll standardize vocabulary and sentence structures. Next, we'll develop a quality assessment model to evaluate the performance of style transfer models. This model will leverage a combination of both automatic and human evaluations, utilizing both intrinsic and extrinsic assessment methods. To train and test our quality assessment model, we'll utilize both a fake dataset and a subset of the constructed sentences. Ultimately, we hope this project will contribute to the improvement of style transfer techniques and help address key challenges in NLP research and development.

The significant disparity in image description quality highlights the need 
for revised guidelines. Accurate descriptions depend on precise context, 
rendering a one-size-fits-all approach ineffective. Machine learning models 
can potentially address this variety, yet current datasets and evaluation 
methods fall short of addressing the diversity of descriptions. To address this 
issue, we propose a method for automatically evaluating the accuracy of image 
descriptions using visual information. This approach leverages a uniquely 
designed dataset for training and evaluation purposes, incorporating both 
high-quality descriptions and flawed counterparts. High-accuracy results from 
using this dataset in visual-based evaluation tasks are presented. Additionally, 
a novel method is introduced for automatically generating accurate image 
descriptions using a generative adversarial network.

To accurately model energy loss functions for tantalum oxides, we must consider local field effects and spin-orbit coupling. However, when using a generic TaO+ cluster as model, these factors have a negligible impact on results. Conversely, they significantly influence energy loss spectra when using a more precise model that accounts for tantalum's multiple oxidation states and lattice environments.

The "The Big Sort" phenomenon, described by William H. Chaftez, refers to the significant trend of people living in areas with populations similar to their own socioeconomically. This trend is particularly noticeable in the United States. A mathematical model is introduced to examine the interplay between socioeconomic sorting and the dissemination of misinformation. Counterintuitively, our findings suggest that misinformation often spreads more quickly in areas with more socially homogeneous populations, particularly in regions where wealthy and poor communities are distant from one another. This model also allows for an in-depth analysis of the impact of social homogeneity on misinformation dissemination in various network structures.

When observing and mimicking a demonstration from a knowledgeable instructor, learners rely heavily on verbal instructions. To understand this interplay, we investigate how speech conveys semantic meaning during teaching tasks. We analyze a vast dataset of instructions spoken while performing tasks and find that the semantic meaning of speech is influenced by the demonstration being followed, as well as parts of the task, and any errors made. Additionally, our findings show that speech often lags behind actions, with a median delay of 1 second. We believe these discoveries will contribute to the development of more realistic and semantically precise models that generate text from vision. To achieve this, we present two models, one using a straightforward combination of text and vision features, and the other employing a generative adversarial network, and provide training data guidelines, including the removal of errors from the dataset. Our approach and resulting model are both valuable for generating coherent text from visual input, making them suitable for a wide range of tasks, including text-to-text language translation and text summarization.

We introduce a novel stochastic gradient descent method called the Stochastic Variational Riemannian Gradient Descent (SVRGD) for optimization problems on Riemannian manifolds. SVRGD significantly enhances the efficiency of the Euler-Arnold equation-based algorithm by leveraging sample average cost and updated parameter values in quantum field theory. By combining these enhancements with the harmonic Riemannian gradient descent algorithm, SVRGD is shown to achieve a substantially faster convergence rate than existing algorithms. Moreover, we establish the convergence properties of SVRGD in both smooth and non-smooth optimization scenarios.

Developing reliable and efficient testing frameworks for conversational systems is crucial, yet it poses significant challenges due to the intricate relationships between inputs, outputs, and context in these systems. Current testing methods primarily focus on isolated aspects of conversational interactions, neglecting the need for a unified framework that leverages the interconnected nature of inputs and responses. In response to these limitations, we introduce a novel testing framework that employs graph-based testing techniques to validate conversational systems through comprehensive, structured tests. This approach represents conversational interactions as interconnected graphs and develops test scenarios that traverse these graphs to ensure the consistency and coherence of our systems. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methodology by applying it to a real-world task – evaluating a popular dialogue agent – and present a customizable testing platform that incorporates our framework for widespread use.

We suffer from the common issue of expressing complex user preferences in real-world recommendation scenarios. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework that combines a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module with graph convolution networks for recommendation. The GAPE module employs two distinct branches to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant information and inputs them into a gated unit, which automatically identifies and prioritizes preferred information. Through the integration of the GAPE module and graph convolution networks, our method leverages both local and global information to refine user preferences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by achieving superior performance in comparison to rival baselines for recommendation tasks.

Formulation theory, initially developed for convex polygons within the context of geometric Joyce's conjecture, has been expanded to address various natural problems and their corresponding formulation dimensions. This paper delves into the analysis of these problems and their formulations for natural versions that utilize sharp cones, in comparison to extended formulations. The study explores the concept of formulation depth and its relation to the dimension of exotic cones. Additionally, the paper provides lower and upper bounds for the formulation dimensions of natural problems utilizing sharp cones, in relation to their corresponding extended formulations. The study ultimately examines the formulation depths of CRAFT, Exotic Cone Formulation (ECF), and Convex Polygon Formulation (CPF) to demonstrate the applicability of these concepts to specific problems.

Neural networks for MRI analysis often excel when their development and application involve similar scenarios. However, their reliability in new situations is uncertain. We investigated the robustness of MRI analysis using 3D brain lesion segmentation and 2D knee cartilage layer segmentation as test cases. Our primary experiment involved training on mixed datasets featuring distinct populations and testing on completely new, unrelated data. The purpose of this experiment was to determine if neural networks could effectively utilize previously unseen data, either with or without labeling. We trained on one population, tested on another, and found that high performance was achievable even in these situations. In the best case, results comparable to those achieved on within-group datasets were possible. We also explored other scenarios involving utility estimation, label efficiency, and a comparison of models. Additionally, we trained and tested models on datasets featuring different anatomies. Our findings are consistent across both types of MRI analysis and have implications for model generalizability in medical imaging.

We introduce a framework for network-based multi-agent optimization issues that are widespread in various applications, including power distribution, transportation, and social networks. A generalized consensus-based optimization algorithm is developed and proven to achieve optimal solutions for problems within this framework, even in the presence of incomplete information due to agent limitations or noisy communications.

The Motivation Dynamics framework has been effectively applied to model various self-driving phenomena in single-agent settings. To expand its capabilities, a multi-agent version of the framework has been developed, fueled by the concept that an agent's actions are driven by the interactions with others in its environment. This paper introduces a key aspect of agent behavior, known as rendezvous, which is achieved when two agents with distinct identities come together. The study explores how the interaction between agents affects identity formation and meeting each other's eyes in a vast space. It demonstrates that even with an unbounded domain, agents can still meet in a single-agent setting with a curved surface, and the framework is robust enough to accommodate changes in the agents' movement patterns. The research provides insights into the meeting phenomenon through in-depth analysis of the functions that facilitate self-meeting behaviors.

Recent studies found the ferromagnetic properties of GdSn3 and the paramagnetic properties of CmSn3. This research focuses on the GdxCm(1-x)Sn3 series with x = 0.5 and x = 0.75, examining the structural, magnetic, and electrical properties. Combining the data from these compounds, trends in magnetic moment and electrical resistance with temperature were identified. For x = 0.5, the Curie-Weiss temperature was extracted, and the resistivity demonstrated a linear relationship with temperature. For x = 0.75, the resistivity showed an increase below the Néel temperature, and the magnetic moment indicated a possible antiferromagnetic component.

Within the framework of QCD, our research explores the interactions of heavy quarks, specifically focusing on the formation of charmed and bottom quarks from gluons. We analyzed the probability of observing a particular sequence of events, where a gluon splits into a quark and an antiquark, and then one of the particles further splits into a heavy quark and a light quark. We calculated the amplitude of these events at a fundamental level of QCD and then developed a functional representation of the outcome in terms of a factorizable expression. Ultimately, our findings provide a precise, factorizable expression of the outcome, which can be utilized for various purposes, including the creation of realistic event generators and the development of more efficient algorithms for simulating these events.

We derive the exchange laws for the standard model of the finite classical Coxeter system Bn through a novel approach that combines the fundamental involutions of the symmetric group Sn with the generalized standard subgroup W(S) of W(Bn). Our results reveal relationships between the exchange laws, the Coxeter length of a element within W(S) and the distribution of its descents. Furthermore, we establish the connection between the latter and the Eulerian partitions of Nn.

We analyzed a large dataset of 46000 quasars from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey to extract details about the large-scale structure of the galaxy universe. By combining the positions of quasars and nearby galaxies, we mapped the shape of the universe on a cosmic scale. We used mathematical models to break down the galaxies into distinct components, known as halos, and studied the sizes, masses, movements, and positions of these components. Our research focused on a specific group of halos that house quasars and galaxies, and we created a comprehensive list of likely candidates. We then used statistical techniques to identify patterns in the positions of quasars and galaxies, and their relationships with each other. Our study revealed a prominent pattern of movement that affects the entire universe, as well as localized patterns of movement and structure. We also used the data to create a detailed image of the universe around us. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the universe on a cosmic scale and offers valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the universe.

Our study highlights the distinctive optical properties of T centres in diamond, specifically their broad spectral diffusion patterns and the role of nitrogen vacancies within them. We employed high-resolution spectroscopy to thoroughly examine T centres and developed a theoretical model to interpret our findings. This model proposes that a T centre's optical properties are influenced by a nearby nitrogen atom's spin state and the likelihood of interacting with a nearby electron. According to our research, T centres generally occupy a particular energy range and display unique optical behaviour. However, some of the T centres also demonstrate broader spectral diffusion patterns due to their interaction with electrons. If isolated, these T centres might serve as quantum bits in a solid-state quantum computer, but our research indicates that many of the T centres are linked and could be used in a quantum network.

While pre-trained object detectors can be leveraged for various tasks, their effectiveness varies significantly depending on the context. For example, Faster R-CNN excels in certain benchmark datasets, yet SSD performs better in other situations. Unfortunately, due to the complexity of object detection, it remains challenging to create a universal feature extraction module that seamlessly adapts to different contexts. In response to this challenge, we present a novel context-aware object detection framework known as CAODNet, which selectively employs context-dependent object detectors based on the input data. By employing an attention mechanism and conditional neural architecture search, CAODNet efficiently identifies optimal object detectors for a given context and produces outstanding results on multiple datasets, surpassing the performance of current state-of-the-art models.

We examine the existence of solutions in an elliptic boundary value problem for a system of equations that contains multiple equations. The existence of a solution in the system is tied to the behavior of the function f_i near the boundary of the given domain Ω. If the function f_i does not behave in a specific manner near the boundary, we find that a solution does not exist. The main argument used to establish this non-existence result involves the use of a lemma that enables the reduction of the system to a single equation and facilitates the use of a blow-up method. The corresponding result for a system of equations that includes v(x) as a coefficient is also established.

We investigate the concentration of conditioned sums of independent Bernoulli random variables, obtaining sharp estimates for a wide range of functions, including convex functions and polynomials. Our approaches are analytical and probabilistic, utilizing concentration inequalities and potential analysis. Specifically, we derive tailored bounds for the hypergeometric distribution and its conditioned version. Additionally, we establish concentration results for convex functions and polynomial functions with respect to their norms. These results are demonstrated to be optimally exponential in many cases. Our research supplements recent findings by Bagnell, Pilioud, and Vusio and provides distinct insights into the concentration of conditioned sums of Bernoulli random variables.

For the symplectic group Sp_2n(K), the conjugacy classes are distinguished by two types of forms: a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form associated with the center of the group, and a non-degenerate skew-symmetric bilinear form that determines the conjugacy class. Based on these forms, we establish the structure of the system of invariants for Sp_2n(K). Additionally, we define the ratio of two non-proportional anisotropic forms as the product of two non-degenerate, anisotropic spaces under the tensor product, resulting in a well-defined map from the set of forms to the set of non-degenerate, anisotropic spaces within the symplectic group Sp_2n(K). This mapping enables the parametrization of anisotropic conjugacy classes through a product of non-degenerate, anisotropic spaces under the tensor product, specifically within the symplectic group Sp_2n(K). Furthermore, we identify a specific subset of anisotropic conjugacy classes, denoted as A_an(Sp_2n(K)), consisting of those classes whose associated forms have a specific property - being isotropic - unless the base field has a specific characteristic or satisfies certain conditions.

The complexity of organ transplantation policies is compounded by incompatibilities, leading to a need for new decision theory that incorporates state variables representing incompatibilities. The lack of solution tools for the resulting general problem limits the analysis of a specific and significant application: kidney allocation policies in the United States. The current approach, based on value iteration, fails to provide insights into the factors influencing acceptance or rejection of organ offers. To address this issue, the existing model is modified to include the history of offers and the subsequent analysis yields new understanding of the policy's behavior. Ultimately, the benefits of modified value iteration are demonstrated through application to the kidney allocation problem.

This study examines the consequences of standard word embeddings treating opposites as equivalents when processing financial text. We selected OppositeNet, a model that explicitly represents opposites, to compare its performance with the conventional method of using word2vec. Our analysis of financial news texts and stock introduction descriptions found that OppositeNet outperformed word2vec in various tasks. Notably, OppiteNet Word2Vec achieved higher similarity ratings for opposites, yet this increase in similarity came at the cost of reduced distinction between synonyms. Our proposed OppositeNet architecture was able to mitigate this loss of synonym distinction. Our results also revealed that OppiteNet Word2Vec effectively identified opposites, synonyms, and hyponyms in financial texts. Furthermore, OppiteNet demonstrated a strong performance compared to the conventional method when evaluating its ability to classify sectors based on stock introduction descriptions. Our code is available at no cost on GitHub.

In wideband communication systems, allocating resources (e.g. time/frequency slots) is a complex task, especially when multiple users are involved. To make allocation more efficient, researchers often use machine learning techniques, but ensuring these techniques themselves are fair and efficient poses another challenge. Here, we develop two optimization problems to solve these fairness and efficiency issues. The first problem, fair-throughput optimization, aims to ensure that allocation is both effective and fair by ensuring that no user is disadvantaged relative to the worst-case situation. The second problem, sum-throughput optimization, focuses on finding the most efficient allocation possible. To solve these problems, we use a particular machine learning model called neural networks and develop algorithms to train these networks. Finally, due to the complexity of solving these problems directly, we use numerical methods to solve related sub-problems.

This paper introduces a novel numerical approach that models the intricate dynamics of the Rayleigh-Benard instability in a way that efficiently manages the complex interplay between localized heat input and convection patterns. To achieve this, a proposed multiscale model divides the system into two distinct regions: a centrally located subdomain modeling convection patterns and surrounding subdomains representing thermal gradients. To model heat transfer between these regions, the authors developed a new nonlocal boundary condition. To solve the model numerically, the authors used a multigrid method. To validate the model, the authors conducted a heat transfer test and studied the dynamics of the Rayleigh-Benard instability in both two- and three-dimensional systems. The resulting convection patterns and associated heat transfer rates showed excellent agreement with previous studies.

In multiagent learning settings, agents must sometimes distinguish between actions that lead to suboptimal cycles of counterattacks and those that are directly inferior. To combat this challenge, we present an iterative elimination theory for single-agent Markov Decision Processes, which enables agents to bypass actions involving self-inflicting wounds through a form of regression. We then extend this concept to multiagent settings and test its effectiveness with two scenarios: one with inconsistent policies and the other with corrupted observations. Our results show that agents using this method learn to shun counterproductive behaviors and adhere to optimal policies, even in the presence of inconsistencies or corrupted observations. Furthermore, our approach yields robust results across various dynamic environments.

We examined the spread of an epidemic within a fully connected random network of N individuals, allowing for the possibility of node connections to change after each infection transmission attempt. This dynamic model incorporates elements of both the SIR and the Cayley tree networks. As the network's connectivity maintains a degree of K connected nodes, we found that the final fraction infected approaches 1 at transmission rates above a threshold, which follows a power law in relation to the rate parameter. Additionally, we observed that the time required to reach a certain fraction infected follows a scale-free pattern. Comparisons have been made with analogous results from Cayley tree networks.

This paper demonstrates the implementation of the DGLAP evolution, which describes the distribution of quarks and gluons as a function of energy, in the context of fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) at different scales. By utilizing the NumPy library, we have developed a prototype fit for PDFs in SymPy, an open-source computer algebra system. Our DGLAP evolution implementation is then connected to the MCFI fit package. We have conducted a preliminary fit for PDFs within the Strong Interaction Physics Group at the University of Colorado Boulder, relying on the MCFI fit package and incorporating DGLAP evolution. This fit involves fitting PDFs to multiple datasets at various energy scales, successfully reconciling the discrepancies. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub, presented in the accompanying documentation.

This study introduces variance reduction based experience replay (VRER), a new perspective on using past data to aid policy gradient estimation. By redefining importance sampling and creating a bridge to unbiased estimates, VRER yields multiple unbiased estimate formulas for desired policy gradients. To demonstrate the value of VRER, it is applied to improve the estimated efficiency of policy gradient estimation in three experience replay contexts. Our approach outperforms existing efficient policy gradient estimation methods in three experience replay scenarios: single trajectory experience replay, batch experience replay, and prioritized experience replay.

Theory of mind refers to the ability to comprehend the mental states of others. In the context of AI, developing capabilities for theory of mind is crucial for various dialog generation tasks, including understanding attitudes, emotions, and intentions in conversations. However, current AI approaches largely lack theoretical foundations and are primarily focused on practical applications. To address this gap, we draw from cognitive psychology and construct three scenarios that can help evaluate an AI's theory of mind in dialog. Specifically, we examine the relationship between theory of mind and three key dialog generation tasks: style transfer, dialog resuming, and sentiment analysis. To further explore the connection between theory of mind and dialog generation, we outline three research hypotheses that can be tested using a combination of empirical data and computational models. We anticipate that by understanding the relationship between theory of mind and dialog generation tasks, we can hopefully devise more effective approaches to developing capable AI.

This paper introduces MG-GLAM, a novel code designed for an extreme computing environment featuring a vast number of processors, each with a small amount of memory. Developed to accelerate an intricate N-body simulation system consisting of a vast number of particles, the MG-GLAM code leverages message-passing parallelization techniques and employs a sophisticated grid-based distribution method to achieve significant performance improvements and memory efficiency. By optimizing computational efficiency and memory usage, the MG-GLAM code outperforms a previous code by approximately two orders of magnitude in terms of the number of processors it can efficiently utilize on a large-scale cluster. Furthermore, the code has the capability to efficiently handle a wide range of complex scenarios, including non-uniform particle distributions and curved boundaries, while maintaining an exceptionally high level of computational accuracy.

The chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE$_\kappa$ for $\kappa\in (0,4)$) law on the upper half-plane Riemann surface is defined, and we show that it evolves in a way that is time-reversal symmetric when considered within the Riemann surface. This leads to the discovery of the imaginary part of a family of analytic functions, which can be used to enumerate the growing number of branches of the evolution. These branches correspond to distinct growth patterns of the SLE and form a non-decreasing stack throughout the evolution.

We've developed WorkingWiki, an extended version of the Wikipedia platform tailored for collaborative document and software development. WorkingWiki introduces a robust revision tracking system that differentiates active revisions based on the roles of contributors, as well as a sophisticated approval process for ensuring the quality of published content and code. Additionally, WorkingWiki incorporates discussion forums specific to individual pages and revisions, alongside a sophisticated search function that takes into consideration the revision history. Our system prioritizes revisions with the support of most contributors, utilizing Poincaré duality to compute the computationally expensive harmonic function that guides this process. WorkingWiki's extended features are implemented using customisable plugins, allowing for seamless integration with existing wiki software. Our system's advantages and potential applications are demonstrated through the development of the Textual User Interface for Java, a notorious example of a software project challenging to maintain due to its extensive history of development.

A linearized approach for studying turbulent reactions has been developed and applied to a wide range of combustion models. It was discovered that the level surface model fits well within this linearized framework and its analysis was completed through the application of Pontryagin's minimum principle. A numerical solver was created and used to analyze both reacting and inactive vortices. The results show that the level surface model produces similar outcomes to those achieved using the reduced order model. Furthermore, an investigation into the structure of the control operator was conducted along with the creation of a numerical code to solve the nonlinear equation. The code was utilized to generate data used in training machine learning algorithms. The purpose of this code development was twofold: it not only solved the nonlinear equation but also produced the data needed to train machine learning algorithms. The code was tested and made available for public use. Researchers exploring the parameters of neutrino properties have discovered the possibility of dark matter properties being influenced by neutrinos. This work delves into the consequences of a scenario where dark matter is composed of two WISPy components: one connected to neutrinos and a second linked to axion-like fields. A three-loop diagram illustrating the interaction between these components, neutrinos, and dark photons through a process known as elastic scattering was previously unidentified. We calculate the precise value of this interaction's coefficient and discuss its implications for the distribution of dark matter, particularly in the case of a neutrino-driven, initial dark matter population. Furthermore, we examine the breakdown of the standard weak interaction hierarchy and the consequences for the neutrino component of dark matter, including the initial population's decay and the eventual dominance of the neutrino-independent component of dark matter. This scenario is linked to the degradation of the weak component of dark matter, leading to the formation of oscillons that could potentially produce distinctive signals in future cosmological simulations.

Within the framework of nonlocal gravity, a newly formulated constitutive relation is presented, and its relation to the shape of galaxy rotation curves is investigated. The nonlocal approach can be restructured to resemble a modified surface tension-inspired model, resulting in a constitutive relation that differs from its conventional Fierz-Pauli counterpart. The implications of this distinct relation on the mass of the fundamental particle associated with the nonlocal parameter are explored and potentially observable effects on the features of galaxy rotation curves are investigated. The nonlocal parameter's value is determined to be $k^2 = 4.5 \, \mbox{microparsecs}^{-2}$ with an estimated percent uncertainty of $10\%$, and the predicted mass of the associated particle is found to be $4.5 \times 10^{-28}$ erg, equivalent to $2.7 \times 10^{-23}$ eV.

The complex interplay between proteins, genetics, and phenotype is the subject of scrutiny in our study. We examine the underlying protein sequence influences that explain relationships between specific genetic variants and traits in diverse species. Focusing on the largest available dataset of annotated protein structures and sequences, we explore the relationships between proteins, genetics, and phenotype. Our research reveals that the explanatory power of proteins for trait-associated SNPs differs significantly across various traits, ranging from no explanatory power for traits like height to almost complete explanation for traits like fly lifespan. We also found that proteins are more likely to explain relationships with SNPs that affect an organism's survival or fertility, and that certain protein functions and pathways are more likely to be associated with specific traits or SNPs. Furthermore, we show that the relationships between proteins and genetics can be used to predict the effects of specific SNPs on traits, even when the exact location of the SNP is unknown.

Our study investigates the creation of strange particles such as K*(892) and ρK* in the ALICE detector, specifically in proton-proton collisions at an 8 TeV energy level. These collisions allow us to examine high-energy physics phenomena more finely than open heavy-flavor processes. By comparing theoretical models, we intend to gain a deeper understanding of how strange particle production is made possible through quark-gluon interactions and to pin down the characteristics of these interactions. We have compiled comprehensive datasets of K* and ρK* particles based on their momentum properties and patterns of production, covering a wide range of centralities and covering the entire transverse sphericity spectrum. These findings are in line with existing research, yet our results are more precise, especially when looking at the production of ρK* particles. We have validated the accuracy of our data by means of simulations using the ALICE detector model.

We examined the connection between low-mass X-ray binaries that contain neutron stars in binary systems and the pulsars that emit radio signals within the Galaxy. Our research built upon a previous study that revealed a significant population of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries in the Galaxy, and we aimed to expand upon this finding. By utilizing survey data from the Kepler space telescope and other observations, we identified 60 pulsars that emit radio signals at low spin frequencies, and we found their spatial distribution was aligned with the plane of the Galaxy, specifically within the bulge region. Furthermore, we discovered that the properties of low-mass X-ray binaries that contain neutron stars and the properties of the radio pulsars exhibited strong similarities, suggesting that both populations share a common origin. Based on our findings, we estimate that the Galaxy is home to approximately one million pulsars that emit radio signals, although only a small fraction of these are discovered, and we propose that low-frequency radio pulsars may be a key indicator of the mass distribution of stellar masses within the Galaxy.

The control that quantum mechanics exerts over chemical reaction barriers can be influenced by the vibrations of molecules. This influence can vary significantly based on the quantum state of the system and the reaction in question. We investigate the potential for controlling specific reaction pathways through the coupling of particular vibrational modes to quantum states, with an emphasis on decaying wavepackets in small molecules. Our study involves analyzing two distinct scenarios: one governed by a decaying two-state system with quantum tunneling, and another characterized by nonlinear reaction dynamics involving multiple states and modes. We examine the dynamics of wavepackets in small molecules, including CO2, N2O, and H2O, by numerically solving their time-dependent Schrödinger equations. The results show that the spatial distribution of quantum states and vibrational modes can be used to predict and control chemical reaction outcomes. Furthermore, we outline a control strategy that leverages the coupling of vibrational modes to quantum states by manipulating the quantum states or vibrational modes individually, or through a combination of both. The effectiveness of this control approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations of wavepacket dynamics in methane, with considerations for implementing control using optical fields.

Improving dialogue system performance is increasingly dependent on large, manually curated datasets. However, the time and resources required to create and utilize these datasets are excessive, a problem that is compounded by the inevitable presence of diversity in dialogue responses. Diversity in this context refers to the need to generate responses that exhibit a wide range of meanings and contents, a task that poses significant challenges for standard sequence generation models. In response to these challenges, a new model called the Semantic Generation Dialogue Model has been developed to generate high-quality, diverse responses. This model leverges a multi-round dialogue approach, employing two interacting networks to successively broaden the semantic scope of its initial prediction. Experimental validation has been conducted, yielding outcomes that surpass existing benchmarks in several key metrics.

For objects below 13M, the influence of angular momentum on the carbon-monoxide snow line and the steam explosion threshold is negligible. However, above a certain angular momentum threshold, the carbon-monoxide snow line expands, leading to a switch from hydrogen burning via the main sequence to blue loop behavior. Within the range of 13M to 16M, the snow line's behavior varies greatly with angular momentum. As a result, the critical curves for mass loss during stellar evolution are affected, especially the transition from the main sequence to the subgiant branch, which is delayed due to increased core radius caused by rapid core rotation. Additionally, the zero-age subgiant branch location spreads out across a wider range of luminosity. The influence of angular momentum becomes even more pronounced within the range of 16M to 20M, ultimately leading to the disruption of zero-age subgiant branch location.

A novel method is proposed for estimating the probability of a particle decaying into other particles by using artificial neural networks, which can efficiently handle complex distributions of hadron properties. This new approach, implemented in the FaFoT framework, leverages genetic algorithms to optimize the network's performance and has been successfully tested on synthetic data and real-world decay problems, including the decay of a heavy quark into a bottom quark and the decay of the $\chi_{b0}$ particle into two gamma rays.

Researchers have long studied the persistent and complex phenomena associated with gamma-ray burst (GRB) remnants, yet the theoretical "jet-afterglow" model has limitations, particularly in capturing the transitions between ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic phases. The existing standard model struggles to accurately describe this phase shift, leading to uncertainties in understanding the physical properties of GRBs. A newly developed, unified model aims to provide a more comprehensive explanation for the afterglow phenomena, covering both the ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic phases. This model builds upon the standard model by incorporating a novel "injection" phase, where energy is continuously released into the environment through jet fragments. Through computational simulations, the model successfully recreates afterglow manifestations across various frequencies and observatories, accurately capturing the evolution of spectra and light curves for both GRBs and gamma-ray sky remnants. By successfully incorporating the effects of relativistic effects, the model reveals that the inner edges of jet orbits become visible through X-ray observations in certain situations, and demonstrates that the ultra-relativistic phase is generally short-lived, while the injection phase can influence both the total energy released and the shape of light curves in certain frequencies.

A bipartite graph can be rendered as a non-overlapping, layered drawing on a plane if its maximum vertex degree exceeds 4, as long as certain specific simple transformations called "splitting vertices" are permitted. The process of drawing the graph involves starting with an initial planar double-crossing drawing of the graph's neighborhood for each vertex of high degree. Then, a sequence of operations is performed, where each operation applies to a vertex connected to its immediate neighbors and transforms the double-crossing drawing caused by that vertex into a single-crossing drawing. The task is achieved through a combination of the Golberg-Shahmonov and the Klaviez-Sedgewick methods for handling the double-crossing drawings.

This study explores the potential benefits of feedback control in a basic bipedal robot walking on uneven terrain. We analyzed the robot's locomotion in both open and closed-loop systems to understand the impact of feedback. Our findings show that closed-loop feedback significantly enhances the robot's performance, resulting in a more stable gait and increased robustness in the face of unexpected terrain changes. Our research indicates that feedback plays a crucial role in maintaining overall stability and that control systems can be designed to ensure the robot's robustness in dynamic environments. Our proposed method successfully incorporates feedback into the controller, leading to a stable and robust gait. Our future work aims to improve the controller's performance further and to apply this research to more complex bipedal robots.

This research investigates the computability properties of specific mathematical structures within the context of an arbitrary infinite field. Initially, we examine power series from an infinite field, equipped with operations that incorporate a total residue map, finding this system non-deterministically decidable when the field in question is finite, and undecidable when the field is infinite. Next, we tackle polynomial rings from an infinite field, modifying Skolem's problem to accommodate this context. Finally, we explore a construct known as the field of formal Laurent series, uncovering both its non-primitively recursive and primitive recursive determinacy profiles.

Recent research exploited memory leaks in cryptographic implementations to achieve precise time measurements, breaching security barriers intended to prevent such measurements. To enhance the accuracy and efficiency of these attacks, a new technique called HyperDegrade is developed. Evaluating HyperDegrade on various implementations of popular cryptographic functions, including RSA and elliptic curve cryptography, it is found that HyperDegrade significantly outperforms existing methods. Specifically, HyperDegrade is shown to achieve a 10-fold improvement in time resolution and a 7-fold decrease in required traces for a specific RSA implementation, and a 20-fold increase in time resolution and a 3-fold decrease in required traces for a specific ECC implementation. Additionally, HyperDegrade's effectiveness is demonstrated across various scenarios and system architectures.

Isotopy classes of certain knotted structures, specifically $4$-valent linked curves with a central branch that is homeomorphic to a ball, have been exhaustively categorized based on their reduced griddable representations. A study reveals that the set of all such knotted structures that can be arranged in an equilateral triangle pattern is nonempty and nontrivial, encompassing an infinite number of distinct isotopy classes. Furthermore, a type of move called the diagonal move is established, which allows for the conversion between knotted structures in an equilateral triangle pattern and a specific type of Grigashvili linked curves. The findings from the study on Grigashvili linked curves have been incorporated into this research.

Given a specific type of mathematical structure, known as a quasi-Hopf algebra, that is associated with a knot, we investigate how combining certain mathematical objects, called cocycles, affects the associated knot invariant. This research yields an integral that can be used to define the knot invariant and helps establish a connection between the Berezin transform and the Drinfeld twist. Furthermore, our findings regarding the integration of cocycles provide valuable insights into the characteristics of the associated knot invariants and mathematically rigorous evidence for an integral that is hypothesized to be associated with a specific type of quasi-Hopf algebra.

We examine the co-ordination of tasks between agents with varying levels of capability. Our research focuses on a scenario where tasks differ in terms of ease or hardness and tasks of similar difficulty must be grouped together. We present three algorithms designed to assign tasks to agents based on their capabilities and capacity for problem-solving. Our simulations test these algorithms in different scenarios and demonstrate how the distribution of tasks affects the decisions made by the agents. Furthermore, we analyse the efficiency of our proposed methods in relation to other existing solutions.

This research involves launching privacy breaches against various vertical federated learning schemes, including protocols that use encryption and privacy-preserving techniques. Our analysis reveals that certain attacks can successfully recover sensitive information, leading to a reevaluation of the privacy and security of vertical federated learning. To address this issue, we propose an enhanced method that combines differential privacy with a search-based approach, demonstrating its efficacy in a real-world scenario.

Deep learning methods typically exhibit poor performance or significant dimensionality increases when used with kernel-based techniques due to the difficulty in exploiting the proposed optimizations. To overcome this challenge, researchers have explored various feature transformation methods, including Random Fourier Features (RFF) and Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), which transform kernel embeddings into lower-dimensional representations while maintaining similarity to the original data. Compared to its counterpart RFF, PRFF boasts an additional order of magnitude in terms of dimension reduction, leading to even greater similarity to the original data. However, both RFF and PRFF fall short of their original goal of achieving a linear relationship in dimensionality. To address this limitation, a novel method titled Exact Fourier Features (EFF) has been developed, precise to a desired integer n, granting linear dimensionality when compared to the original data. Notably, EFF's underlying mechanism is analogous to PRFF, thereby extending the applicable scope to include PRFF. The EFF approach is accompanied by a software package called eff for easy implementation.

A key concept in the study of regular group actions and diagonal groups is covered by regular diagonal group actions, a subclass of regular transitive group actions. A group G acts on a Cartesian product X = A × B if the action is defined by g(a, b) = (α(g)a, β(g)b) for some subgroup actions α and β of G on A and B, respectively. If A and B are nontrivial then we say the action is diagonal. Our main result shows that any group action on a product space can be decomposed into a chain of diagonal actions on product spaces, a finding we call Cartesian Decomposition. This decomposition is unique and takes the form Z ×∅ if the action is trivial, or yields a chain of diagonal actions on products of nontrivial spaces if the action is not trivial. Our proof of Cartesian Decomposition relies on an earlier result of Grsueld and Lenagle, as well as the more recent work of Grsueld, Lenagle and Soule.

We establish an infinite sequence of lower bounds for the M\"obius scalar curvature of compact conformally flat hypersurfaces within certain dimensional ranges. Specifically, for even-dimensional settings equal to four or more, we can demonstrate that there exist positive constants enabling the following inequality to be sustained: $\frac{R_{\text{conf}}}{r^2}\frac{\sigma_2(\Gamma)^2}{A_{n-1}(\Gamma)}\geq \frac{C_1(n)}{R_{\text{conf}}}\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)^{2n}$, where $r$ represents a scale parameter, $R_{\text{conf}}$ denotes the conformally flat scalar curvature, $\sigma_2(\Gamma)$ and $A_{n-1}(\Gamma)$ are geometric parameters associated with the hypersurface, and $C_1(n)$ is a dimension-dependent constant. Furthermore, we derive an upper limit for the M\"obius operator and employ this result to demonstrate the existence of a positive lower bound for the M\"obius scalar curvature in specific dimensional settings, with values varying across these settings.

A novel energy-efficient strategy called Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (GAST) is proposed for a specific type of network that transfers information and energy simultaneously, known as SWIPT networks. The purpose of GAST is to dynamically switch between different antennas based on varying channel conditions, in order to optimize performance and conserve energy. In order to analyze the performance of GAST, an mathematical model is developed and used to identify its optimal policy. Furthermore, GAST is compared to a current energy-efficient technique called Adaptive Antenna-Switching Technique (AAST), and shows that GAST outperforms AAST in terms of data transfer rate and is more energy-efficient. Additionally, GAST is applied to a problem where a base station needs to transfer data to multiple receivers, and this is shown to be a feasible solution.

Researchers studied the spread of damage through complex networks that don't follow random patterns. They analyzed the impact of small disturbances growing into large events and found that networks prone to big crashes aren't necessarily fragile. Instead, the outcome often depends on how damage spreads in stages. For example, scientists found that removing a single node in a specific network resulted in tiny shocks becoming much more likely to grow, but the probability returned to normal after just two nodes were removed. On the other hand, networks that do crash badly don't always spread destruction evenly. In some cases, the physical location of node connections affects how damage spreads, and scientists found that the shape of networks can be misleading, appearing fragile but actually resisting change, like the ring network that survived node removal, not fragmentation, but rather node failure.

Quantum interference phenomena have been utilized to enhance sensitivity in physical measurements. A recently proposed interferometer arrangement, known as the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, demonstrates an even greater sensitivity improvement. This new design builds upon the concept of the sloshing-MZI interferometer, incorporating a coherent quantum process that amplifies metric variations and thus significantly boosts metrological precision. Compared to traditional interferometers, the sloshing-Sagnac design achieves an marked sensitivity enhancement, exhibiting a 4-fold increase in the coefficient defining its sensitivity to the parameter of interest. Furthermore, due to the unique physics it leverages, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer exhibits an enhanced sensitivity to gravitational fields, with a coefficient 4 times greater than a standard Sagnac interferometer of equal size.

This paper proposes a new random access (RA) protocol called NOVR-XL to address scalability issues in massive MIMO (MIMO) systems. By reducing control channel loads, NOVR-XL significantly enhances random access performance and decreases latency. To evaluate NOVR-XL's effectiveness, we simulate a massive MIMO system with up to 256 antennas and 64 users, incorporating realistic, detailed models of channel behavior, power management, and scheduling. Our results show that NOVR-XL substantially improves random access efficiency, supporting up to 256-element arrays for user detection and base station semi-annual upgrades with minimal performance degradation. Furthermore, NOVR-XL reduces latency by facilitating rapid initial access and minimizing retransmissions. Our research demonstrates the feasibility and advantages of NOVR-XL in state-of-the-art massive MIMO systems.

Bistatic radio holography is an imaging technique that reconstructs objects from the interference patterns of scattered waves. This method can be applied to protoplanetary disks imaged through interferometry, allowing researchers to visualize substructures within the disks' outer regions. By interpreting these substructures as potential sites for planetesimal formation, they may, in turn, lead to the formation of planets. The $ALMA$ archival data contain extensive information that, using this bistatic approach, reveals a prominent substructure in the outer regions of the HK Corriolis disk, specifically in the outer 30 AU region. The detected features align with previous findings from other observations and simulations. The likely explanation for the disk's unusual shape involves a massive gravitationally bound object with a minimum mass 10 times greater than that of our planet. The findings also suggest the presence of a massive satellite or a massive, rapidly orbiting disk fragment with a possible impact on the formation and evolution of the surrounding environment.

A recently developed energy density functional, known as BigApple, has been enhanced to better suit large scale nuclear applications. Originally derived from an interaction based approach, the BigApple functional was modified to conform to the constraints of density functional theory. To assess the nuclear matter properties associated with this functional, we calculated the equation of state for nuclear matter. By evaluating the energy per particle relative to the binding energy per nucleon of the ground state, we gathered information about the nuclear matter properties connected with BigApple. Furthermore, a modified version of the functional, called BigApple-M, was developed to enhance the accuracy of the results. BigApple-M was created by adjusting the Fock term of BigApple to ensure that the associated nuclear matter properties align with established, empirical values. Comparative analysis revealed that the BigApple-M version of the energy density functional offers an improved representation of the nuclear matter equation of state, specifically with respect to the saturation point. Additionally, BigApple-M was found to be in closer agreement with the results provided by the well-established Skyrme interaction. To visualize the associated effects, we used BigApple and BigApple-M to calculate odd-even mass differences, neutron star masses, and neutron star maximum masses.

Our investigation focuses on the performance of frequency-robust Molmer-Sorensen gates within trapped ion systems. To better understand how variations in frequency affect the outcome, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the robust Molmer-Sorensen gate's design. Compared to a conventional Molmer-Sorensen gate, we found that the frequency-robust version exhibits a significantly slower entanglement accumulation rate in small-scale systems, although this difference becomes less pronounced in larger systems. In order to mitigate this issue, we propose an alternative design featuring a notational "swap" operation that is directly comparable to the conventional Molmer-Sorensen gate, yet exhibits a distinct operational dynamics. Through numerical data, we observed that the alternative design yields the same level of entanglement accumulation as the conventional Molmer-Sorensen gate, while maintaining the benefit of frequency robustness.

A recently discovered material, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$, exhibits both Dirac electrons and strong many-body physics, making it an intriguing subject for study. This material's unique crystal structure suggests the presence of both direct and indirect interactions between electrons, facilitating the realization of a Weyl semi-metal state. In the present study, we employ an efficient kernel-based method to evaluate the impact of many-body effects on the electronic properties of GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of realizing a Weyl semi-metal state in this material by analyzing the band structure along high-symmetry directions and localized electron orbitals. Additionally, we explore the potential of this material to host both Weyl nodes and a semi-metallic state, and discuss the prospects of experimental verification through Weyl-Lorentz effect and Weyl point anomaly.

The search for heavy neutral leptons is a pressing concern, and their possible elusion from current experiments makes their discovery even more crucial for future experiments. NUSTAR at the European Nuclear Physics Laboratory (CERN) employed a 1.85 GeV beam of gold ions to scan for heavy neutral leptons within certain mass ranges. Utilizing two detectors, TIRA and CRAFT, with distinct sensitivities, NUSTAR combined their findings to narrow the detection limits for heavy neutral leptons with small neutrino content or large neutrino content. For the latter case, the new limit stands at 2.5 kiloelectronvolts, with a probability of 90% confidence. On the other hand, the current limit for the former case is already nearing the expected value from neutrino oscillation experiments. Future experiments are positioned to bridge this gap, as the discovered window allows for innovative ideas in particle and nuclear physics research.

Recent advancements in neural language modeling have revolutionized the field, and when combined with basic N-gram models, has led to significant improvements in various language tasks including machine translation and summarization. One effective method of enhancing performance is to create a hybrid model that leverages the strengths of both neural language models and basic N-gram models. Fifty years have passed since the initial proposal of such a concept by Jelinek, and to honour this milestone, this paper delves into a straightforward yet efficient implementation of a hybrid model consisting of a neural language model and a weighted finite-state transducer N-gram model. The integration process is done through weighted integration of the substructures, and the resulting model is trained using maximum likelihood estimation. The proposed hybrid model was tested on a subtask of the WMT 2014 English-to-German news translation and the DUC 2004 summarization task, and the findings showed a notable improvement in performance over the individual models.

Reconstructing a 3D face relies on representing it as a combination of appearance-dependent and independent factors. Prior approaches typically estimate the 3D face directly from images, neglecting the underlying factor structure. In contrast, a proposed framework, known as the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), decomposes the representation into two sub-representations, one for each factor, and enforces alignment through a unique dual structure. Unlike existing methods that reconstruct faces from frontal views, SARDNet seeks to recover faces from a variety of angles, leveraging a novel dual regression framework that estimates both the face under illumination and the albedo from a single image. High-quality reconstructions are achieved with the proposed method, and notable improvements are found in the Aligned Face Dataset with orientations other than front-facing, along with the Face Recension 2020 baseline challenge, which prioritizes front-facing faces.

Researchers have discovered that, under certain conditions, a negative potential value can be generated on a large scale due to a particular feature in the inflationary context. They identified that this phenomenon is linked to a specific pattern of large-scale density fluctuations, characterized by a specific alignment of positive and negative values of the Bardeen potential.
